abstract: |
  Sustainable high-performance computing requires energy measurements that
  remain attributable to program phases, comparable across configurations, and
  auditable after execution. This paper presents a solver-neutral Python
  workflow that couples Gurobi and SCIP to PaScal Analyzer on an HPC system.
  Declarative experiment matrices define five capacitated
  facility-location instances, three solver profiles, controlled core
  treatments, six attempts per configuration, and hierarchical regions for
  model loading and solve execution. Sampled RAPL power is integrated only
  after fail-closed validity checks and compared with a separately acquired
  global RAPL reading, assessing internal consistency rather than absolute
  sensor accuracy. A companion adaptation of PaScal Viewer derives and
  visualizes regional energy from the validated samples. The corrected

  results demonstrate a bounded, reproducible research MVP in the evaluated

# Introduction

Mathematical optimization experiments commonly emphasize solve time,
optimality gap, and solution quality. Energy is increasingly relevant to
sustainable high-performance computing (HPC), but a single process may include
model loading, solver initialization, optimization, and output handling. A
credible study must therefore bind measurements to explicit execution regions,
record the experimental context, and reject malformed telemetry instead of
silently repairing it. This places the work directly in energy monitoring and
observability rather than in the design of a new optimization algorithm.

Intel Running Average Power Limit (RAPL) interfaces expose model-based energy
information for processor domains [@rotem2012rapl]. PaScal Suite combines an
Analyzer for controlled execution and measurement with a Viewer for exploring
scalability data [@silva2025pascalsuite; @silva2019pascalviewer]. The challenge
addressed here is to connect Python solver APIs to PaScal's native manual-region
mechanism, validate sampled energy, and carry the regional semantics through to
visual analysis without making the workflow specific to one solver.

We present Python support/extension to PaScal Suite (Parallel Scalability
Suite), a research prototype that executes Gurobi and SCIP through a common
experiment contract. The study asks:

1. **RQ1:** Can both solvers use the same declarative experiment and regional
   telemetry contract while retaining native solver semantics?
2. **RQ2:** Does integrated sampled RAPL energy agree with a separately acquired
   global RAPL reading within a median absolute relative difference of 5%?
3. **RQ3:** Do accepted configurations remain within a preferred 10%
   coefficient-of-variation threshold after invalid attempts are disclosed and
   rejected?
4. **RQ4:** Under matched dataset, profile, partition, allocation, and one-core
   conditions, what descriptive time-and-energy differences are observed?

The contribution is an end-to-end measurement, visualization, and evidence
pipeline: solver adapters, native region instrumentation, validity gates,
PaScal Viewer energy support, provenance manifests, processed research data,
comparison tables, and a publication workflow.

# Background and Related Work

## Energy measurement and sustainable HPC

RAPL originated in Intel's Sandy Bridge power-management architecture and
provides processor-domain energy information [@rotem2012rapl]. It is not a
facility-energy meter, and exposed domains depend on the machine and operating
system. We therefore restrict claims to the declared PaScal RAPL domain.

Energy research spans measurement, modeling, and resource control. Da Silva et
al. model HPC application energy as a function of workload, clock frequency,
and active cores, reporting that application-specific controls can reduce
energy but require empirical characterization [@silva2022analytical]. At the
system level, Springborg et al. move energy awareness into a Slurm plugin for
automatic job scheduling [@springborg2023slurm]. Our work is complementary: it
produces phase-attributed, validated observations that may support later models
or scheduling policies, but it neither predicts energy nor changes scheduling.

A systematic review found the evidence connecting software design choices to
energy performance to be limited and sometimes contradictory, emphasizing the
need for reproducible empirical studies [@bree2025softwaredesign]. Accordingly,
we publish validity rules, provenance, processed results, and bounded claims.

## PaScal, solvers, and benchmarks

PaScal Suite evaluates shared-memory scalability and records multiple
performance dimensions [@silva2025pascalsuite]. PaScal Viewer was introduced to
make scalability trends navigable through interactive visualizations
[@silva2019pascalviewer]. The Analyzer version evaluated here exposes a global
RAPL value and a sampled RAPL power series [@pascal2026]. Their agreement gives
an internal consistency check, while the Viewer adaptation described below
makes the validated regional energy inspectable.

Gurobi is accessed through its Python API [@gurobi2026manual]. SCIP is accessed
through PySCIPOpt and retains its native constraint-integer-programming
semantics [@hojny2025scip]. Profile names align experimental intent, not
algorithms: defaults, presolve, and warm-start acceptance remain solver
specific.

The workload subset comes from the MILPBench hard split [@ye2025milpbench]: five
capacitated facility-location instances numbered 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25.
Facility-location MILP research also includes robust formulations, uncertainty
sets, and Benders decomposition [@haq2025facilitylocation]. Those variants are
outside this experiment; the citation identifies a broader problem space and a
limit on external validity.

# System Design

The workflow has four layers. A YAML document declares solver, workloads,
resources, repetitions, profiles, telemetry policy, and output directory. A
solver-neutral adapter creates a PaScal Analyzer batch whose application is a
native ELF proxy. A solver-specific Python runner loads the model, applies a
profile, optimizes it, and records metadata. Validation tools then reject
invalid telemetry, consolidate accepted runs, compare matched matrices, and
export portable evidence.

The native proxy is necessary because the evaluated PaScal build records manual
regions when instrumentation calls originate in the process launched by the
Analyzer. A guarded inter-process protocol lets the Python runner request
boundaries without rewriting Analyzer output; the Analyzer JSON remains the
telemetry authority.

Both solvers share three hierarchical regions:

| Region | Operational meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | Complete runner pipeline |
| 0.1 | Model read/build phase |
| 0.2 | Solve execution |

The common profiles are `default`, `presolve-off`, and `warm-start`. Gurobi uses
supported start representations including MST files; SCIP uses SOL files,
optionally gzip-compressed. The workflow verifies identity and association but
does not assume algorithmic equivalence between native starts.

PaScal Suite natively uses the `rapl-sysfs` metric for hardware power
consumption and energy-efficiency monitoring on Linux. The Linux Intel RAPL
kernel driver abstracts these counters through the powercap framework, exposing
the data to user space through the sysfs directory tree at
`/sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl`. Figure 1 shows PaScal Viewer
renderings of the resulting normalized `rapl-sysfs` energy maps.

The corrected `rapl-sysfs` Viewer artifact was produced from the Gurobi
`default` profile with explicit minimization and a 300-second solver budget.
The columns `i1`, `i2`, `i3`, `i4`, and `i5`
correspond, respectively, to MILPBench hard capacitated facility-location
instances 5, 10, 15, 20, and 25. The rows labeled 1, 2, and 4 denote both the
PaScal resource count and the corresponding Gurobi `Threads` setting. Six
repetitions were executed for each core-instance configuration, for a total of
90 attempts. The SCIP comparison uses the same five instances and the one-core
treatment, but it is not represented in this Gurobi-only heatmap.

Region 0.1 covers model loading through the native Gurobi API (`gp.read`),
rather than algebraic model generation, whereas Region 0.2 contains only the
optimization call (`model.optimize`). Profile configuration and
initial-solution loading occur inside the enclosing Region 0 but outside Regions
0.1 and 0.2. PaScal Viewer labels these regions as 0.0.1 and 0.0.2 because it
prefixes the Analyzer region paths with its whole-program root. Each heatmap
cell therefore represents the regional `rapl-sysfs` energy associated with
one core-instance configuration. For visualization, the Viewer normalizes each
instance independently across its available core treatments to a 0--100 scale;
the underlying joule measurements remain in the checksummed evidence.

![PaScal Viewer normalized `rapl-sysfs` energy maps for model loading (Region
0.0.1) and optimization (Region 0.0.2) from the corrected Gurobi `default`
campaign with explicit minimization and a 300-second solver budget. The Viewer
prefixes Analyzer regions 0.1 and 0.2 with its whole-program root.](manuscript/figures/pascal-viewer-regional-energy.png){#fig-viewer width=100%}

## Viewer adaptation

The PaScal Viewer parser was extended to detect `rapl_sample-*` sensors, derive
the canonical `rapl-*` domain, and integrate power over the union of each
region's time intervals using the trapezoidal rule. It preserves legacy
regional-energy maps and hierarchical identifiers, rejects a complete sampled
series when power or timestamps violate the validity contract, falls back to
valid samples when a global scalar is non-positive, and does not mutate the
Analyzer JSON. The implementation and nine focused parser tests are identified
by Viewer commit `e78e96ff` and GitLab MR !15.^[Viewer repository:
<https://gitlab.com/lappsufrn/pascalsuite-viewer>.]

# Experimental Method

The experimental unit is one attempt for a workload, profile, and solver-core
treatment. Each configuration has six attempts and requires at least five valid
runs. Gurobi used one, two, and four solver cores; the cross-solver comparison
uses the common one-core treatment. Final campaigns ran on the NPAD `intel-128`
partition with exclusive allocation requested and Slurm reporting
`OverSubscribe=NO`. Manifests record clean worktrees, software versions,
scheduler metadata, and hashes for configurations, workloads, and starts.
Gurobi 13.0.2 and SCIP 10.0 through PySCIPOpt 6.2.1 were evaluated.

The source LP files declare maximization, whereas the intended capacitated
facility-location experiment is minimization. Both runners therefore record the
source objective direction, explicitly apply minimization after native model
loading, and verify the effective direction before optimization. Every attempt
uses a 300-second native solver limit. Consequently, reported region-0.2
measurements characterize fixed-budget optimization rather than time to proven
optimality.

The Python validator requires finite non-negative power, sorts timestamps,
retains the last sample at duplicate timestamps, and rejects gaps exceeding
three median sampling periods. It requires at least two distinct samples and
finite positive global energy. Boundary extrapolation uses constant endpoint
power for at most one median period; insufficient coverage is rejected. Invalid
attempts are retained with reasons and excluded without correction or
imputation. Whole-program sampled energy is trapezoidally integrated and
compared with global PaScal RAPL energy. A profile passes when median absolute
relative error is at most 5%; the preferred repeatability gate requires maximum
configuration-level coefficient of variation (CV) at most 10%. Regional energy
is integrated only after run-level checks. The reported CV concerns region 0
energy, not region 0.2 alone; the consistency difference concerns the whole
program. For RQ4, time, energy, and
energy-delay product (EDP) refer to region 0.2, with ratios computed as SCIP
divided by Gurobi. The analysis is descriptive; no hypothesis test is reported.

# Results

## Matrix validity

| Solver | Profile | Valid / attempted | Median error (%) | Maximum CV (%) |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Gurobi | default | 84 / 90 | 0.309447 | 1.031979 |
| Gurobi | presolve-off | 84 / 90 | 0.317460 | 0.779982 |
| Gurobi | warm-start | 83 / 90 | 0.315904 | 0.812490 |
| SCIP | default | 29 / 30 | 0.246062 | 3.236270 |
| SCIP | presolve-off | 28 / 30 | 0.288293 | 10.538866 |
| SCIP | warm-start | 28 / 30 | 0.240095 | 0.784039 |

All profile matrices passed the mandatory gate. The largest median consistency
error was 0.317460%, well inside the 5% threshold. The maximum CV was 10.538866%
for SCIP `presolve-off`, slightly above the preferred, non-binding 10% target;
the other five profiles remained below it. The campaign produced 362 physical
attempts and a 360-row logical matrix. Twenty-four logical attempts were invalid,
and every configuration retained the required five valid observations.

The SCIP default/instance-15 cell initially retained only four valid attempts.
Two independent attempts were collected under the same contract and both
passed telemetry validation. A deterministic compositor replaced the two
invalid positions chronologically. Selection used only telemetry validity and
did not consider solver outcome, energy, duration, objective, bound, gap, or
node count. No measured value was corrected or imputed, and the original,
retry, and composition artifacts remain checksummed.

## Controlled one-core comparison

Fifteen matched configurations combine five workloads and three profiles. The
corrected comparison gate verifies dataset fingerprints, profile contracts,
effective minimization, the 300-second native solver budget, partition,
exclusive allocation, clean source worktrees, and accepted input matrices.

| Profile | Duration ratio | Energy ratio | EDP ratio |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| default | 1.069927 | 0.995437 | 1.064858 |
| presolve-off | 1.011974 | 0.958652 | 0.970521 |
| warm-start | 1.072602 | 1.000150 | 1.072563 |

Ratios are SCIP divided by Gurobi and are medians over the five paired
instance-level ratios for each profile. Under `default`, SCIP used 0.46% less
regional energy while taking 6.99% longer, yielding 6.49% higher EDP. Under
`presolve-off`, SCIP used 4.13% less energy while taking 1.20% longer, yielding
2.95% lower EDP. Under `warm-start`, energy was effectively equal (0.015%
higher for SCIP), while duration and EDP were approximately 7.26% higher.
These are fixed-budget regional-telemetry comparisons; they do not show time to
proven optimality or equivalent terminal solution quality.

These telemetry gates do not establish equivalent terminal solution quality.
The status and objective of each included run require a separate audit. Native
sentinel values such as SCIP `-1e20` and `1e20` indicate unavailable bounds or
gaps and are not scientific measurements. Missing gaps must not be inferred as
zero, and the hard-split label does not establish difficulty for either solver.

# Discussion

RQ1 is supported operationally: both solvers completed the same declarative
profile and region contract, and the preceding PaScal Viewer figure renders the
resulting hierarchy and energy domain. This is interface parity, not
algorithmic equivalence. RQ2 and RQ3 are supported within the design: the two
RAPL paths agreed closely, and variability remained below the preferred bound
after transparent run rejection. The fail-closed policy matters because
negative or insufficiently covered series occurred even in completed jobs.

RQ4 supports only a bounded fixed-budget telemetry comparison, not a universal
ranking or a time-to-optimality claim. Native defaults, presolve, start
semantics, and campaign timing remain possible causes. The corrected ratios are
close to parity: SCIP duration is 1.20%--7.26% higher, whereas regional energy
ranges from 4.13% lower to 0.015% higher. The resulting EDP changes direction
across profiles, from 2.95% lower under `presolve-off` to 7.26% higher under
`warm-start`. This profile dependence reinforces the systematic-review warning
that software-energy findings require explicit context
[@bree2025softwaredesign]. It also illustrates why phase-level telemetry is
useful: changes in solver configuration can alter solve energy separately from
model loading. These observations could parameterize energy models such as
[@silva2022analytical] or inform schedulers such as
[@springborg2023slurm], but predictive modeling and scheduling intervention
remain future work.

The end-to-end execution in a relevant HPC environment, including visual
inspection and portable evidence, supports a TRL 5 prototype and a bounded TRL
6 demonstration of the validated configuration. It does not establish
production readiness.

# Threats to Validity

**External validity.** Evidence covers one deterministic facility-location
family, five instances, one cluster partition, and recorded solver versions.
Robust and decomposition-based formulations surveyed in
[@haq2025facilitylocation], other MILP families, hardware, and energy domains
require replication.

**Internal validity.** Same-partition exclusive allocation and manifests reduce
interference and drift, but solvers ran in separate jobs, leaving temporal and
node effects. The selective SCIP telemetry retry introduced another temporal
block; its chronological, outcome-independent composition rule mitigates but
does not remove that threat.

**Construct validity.** RAPL represents processor-domain rather than facility
energy. Region boundaries include wrapper/API overhead; EDP is defined only
for the solve region. Viewer visualization validates interpretability, not
sensor accuracy independently of Analyzer data.
Both acquisition paths share RAPL; agreement therefore establishes internal
consistency, not external-meter accuracy or independently validated regional
attribution. RAPL update timing and non-atomic reads can affect measurements
[@khan2018rapl].

**Statistical validity.** Six attempts provide redundancy for invalid
telemetry but limited inferential power. Medians, ratios, and CVs are
descriptive. Native defaults, presolve, and starts match intent rather than
algorithmic treatment.

# Reproducibility and Availability

The repository contains experiment contracts, launchers, validators, tests,
manuscript source, the publication figure, and machine-readable processed
results. The processed tables reproduce every aggregate reported here and
record campaign commits, scheduler jobs, partition, allocation policy, and
software versions. Raw HPC telemetry, licensed material, benchmark archives,
and large solver-start files remain outside Git; the evidence exporter removes
cluster-local paths and emits checksummed portable packages.

The current GitHub repository contains the software and machine-readable
processed tables, while the Zenodo software record preserves the `v0.1.0`
source release. A separate Zenodo evidence dataset retains all 360 attempts,
including accepted and rejected measurements, together with sanitized Analyzer
outputs, manifests, processed tables, checksums, and reconstruction scripts.
Administrative paths and hosts are redacted; benchmark instances, solver
licenses, and warm-start files are excluded. Both records use the MIT License.

The manuscript uses Quarto [@quarto2026]. Pull requests render HTML, SBC PDF,
and retained LaTeX, then run citation and PDF checks. GitHub Pages is published
only from reviewed `main`.

# Conclusion

PaScal Suite Python demonstrates reproducible regional energy observability for
Gurobi and SCIP on HPC infrastructure. Corrected fixed-budget campaigns met the
mandatory accuracy and replication gates; five of six profiles also met the
preferred repeatability target, with the remaining exceedance disclosed.
PaScal Viewer made regional energy inspectable, and 15 matched one-core
configurations were exported as processed research data. This bounded MVP
addresses measurement and observability for sustainable HPC. Broader claims
require additional problem families, systems, versions, randomized campaign
scheduling, and inferential analysis.
